extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic theory and political reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what properly constitutes a democratic state and how a democratic government ought to act—covering sovereignty, equality, opportunities, public spirit, and the proper scope and aims of state intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular sovereignty as ultimate responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "Ultimate responsibility for the government of a community must reside somewhere."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If divine or royal sovereignty is rejected a polity must acknowledge popular sovereignty; countries that discard monarchy (e.g., France, United States) cannot logically avoid some form of ultimate popular power. England evaded by compromise/legal fiction (parliamentary sovereignty), but republics must recognize ultimate responsibility in the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy must express the sovereign will in ways that preserve its own continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Democracy must at least mean an expression of the Sovereign will, which will not contradict and destroy the continuous existence of its own Sovereign power."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The popular will must be expressed so as to secure the perpetuity and integrity of democratic institutions. Examples and anti-patterns: French assemblies elected by universal suffrage sometimes adopted reactionary or undemocratic policies; plebiscites have delegated sovereignty to dictators—these are instances of popular will exercised against democracy's self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal rights for all; no permanent legal privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Government by the people has its natural and logical complement in government for the people—Lincoln's formulation as 'equal rights for all and special privileges for none.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An essentially democratic state must grant and secure rights equally; systemic, permanent legal privileges for any class violate core democratic principle. The ideal: all citizens enjoy legally defined rights equally (a 'Square Deal').

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal equality is distinct from (and insufficient for) equality of opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although rights may be equal under the law, 'there cannot possibly be any equal opportunities' when material conditions (wealth, education, training) advantage some individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both formal legal equality and the material conditions shaping opportunities. The text uses the marathon analogy: identical starting marks do not ensure equal chances if nourishment/training differ. Policy must recognize that equal legal rights do not automatically produce equal opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic principle should promote mutual forbearance and loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental democratic principle should, above all, counsel mutual forbearance and loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formative democratic idea must bind, heal, and unify public opinion. The bare formula of equal rights can be confusing and disintegrating, encouraging suspicion, demagoguery, and factionalism. Good democratic policy fosters mutual ties deeper than differences of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: The state must assert national responsibility (constructive discrimination)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation 'has to have a will and a policy'—the national public interest must be affirmed by positive action rather than mere non-interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Democracies cannot remain purely neutral; they must select among ways people exercise rights to promote national perpetuity and integrity. This may require deliberate, constructive discrimination (active policies) rather than passive acceptance of natural selection. Examples: protective tariffs, Interstate Commerce Act, Pure Food Bill, factory legislation—these are forms of artificial preference enacted to serve broader national or social interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that both action and inaction are forms of selection
rubrics_metrics.description: "The practice of non-interference is just as selective in its effects as the practice of state interference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers must admit that choosing not to intervene is itself a policy that selects outcomes. Thus the question is not neutrality vs interference per se, but which selection better serves national welfare; prefer policies that learn from mistakes and intelligently choose between natural and artificial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statesmanship may legitimately abandon judicial-style impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Impartiality is the duty of the judge rather than the statesman; the state 'must on the whole make the rules in its own interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A democratic government acting as a statesman need not feign perfect impartiality; it should shape rules that favor national welfare and those likely to use advantages for the public good (analogy: bank at Monte Carlo). This is an explicit rebuttal to strict Jeffersonian non-interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference must be purposive: balance liberty and equality
rubrics_metrics.description: When the state interferes it must decide whether to act on behalf of individual liberty, social equality, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This raises an explicit evaluative criterion for policy: the aim of interference must be defined (protecting liberty, achieving equality, or reconciling both). Historical positions (Hamiltonian national responsibility vs Jeffersonian liberty/non-interference) serve as contrasting norms; democratic judgment must choose and justify which objective is being pursued.
